title: Distributed rate limiting with Redis and Lua

items.stem: Your API runs on 4 servers behind a load balancer. A limiter keeps each client's count in a Python dict inside each server. What is wrong with this design?

options.text: Each server enforces its own limit, so one client gets about four times the intended rate
Python dicts cannot be updated by more than one request at the same moment in time
The load balancer sums every server's counter and so rejects clients too early
Counters kept in memory are lost on each request and so never reach the limit

items.stem: A developer runs GET on a client's token count, decides in Python, then runs SET with the new count, as three separate Redis commands. Each Redis command is atomic. Why can the limiter still over-allow?

options.text: Redis may run the commands out of order, so the SET can be applied first
Another server's commands can run between the GET and the SET of this one
Redis forgets the value after a GET until a later SET has been received
A SET command is atomic only when it is sent from a single server alone

items.stem: A token bucket has capacity 8 and refills at 4 tokens per second. A client's stored bucket holds 3 tokens, and the next request (cost 1) arrives exactly 2 seconds after the last update. After the refill is applied and the request is allowed, how many tokens are stored?
Your Lua rate-limit script needs the current time. Should it take the time from the API server that calls it or from Redis itself, and why, in one sentence?
A client exceeds its limit. Which response best fits good REST API design?

options.text: Status 200 with an error message in the body, since the request arrived
Status 500 with a generic message, since the server declined the request
Status 429 with a Retry-After header and your standard JSON error body
Status 404 with an empty body, since the server hides the resource now
